note.explanation: Avogadro's number, Nₐ, is 6.022 × 10²³. It tells us how many units—such as atoms or molecules—are in one mole of a substance. A mole is an amount of substance; Avogadro's number is the number of units in that amount.
examples: 1 mole of carbon atoms contains 6.022 × 10²³ carbon atoms.
2 moles of water molecules contain 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ water molecules.
note.checkAnswer: One mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ units; Avogadro's number is that count.
note.simple: A mole is a counting amount, like a dozen. Instead of 12 items, one mole contains 6.022 × 10²³ units.
note.checkQuestion: How many molecules are in one mole of a substance?
note.title: Avogadro's Number and the Mole
steps: Identify whether the question asks for atoms, molecules or moles.
To find units, multiply moles by Nₐ.
To find moles, divide the number of units by Nₐ.

mcqs.stem: How many atoms are in 1 mole of neon atoms?
rationales: Correct: one mole contains Avogadro's number of units, so 1 mole of neon atoms contains 6.022 × 10²³ atoms.
This is half of Avogadro's number and would represent 0.5 mole of atoms.
This is twice Avogadro's number and would represent 2 moles of atoms.
Twelve is the number in a dozen, not the number in a mole.

mcqs.stem: How many molecules are present in 1 mole of carbon dioxide?
rationales: Correct: one mole of any molecular substance contains 6.022 × 10²³ molecules.
Carbon dioxide is made of molecules, so this gives the wrong kind of unit.
This is half the number of molecules in one mole.
The formula CO₂ has three atoms per molecule, but that does not mean one mole has only two molecules.

The exponent is one power of ten too small.
This is not Avogadro's number.
This could be a molar mass in grams per mole for oxygen molecules, but it is not a particle count.

mcqs.stem: A sample contains 3.011 × 10²³ atoms. How many moles of atoms does it contain?
rationales: One mole contains twice as many atoms as this sample.
Two moles contain four times as many atoms as this sample.
Correct: 3.011 × 10²³ is half of 6.022 × 10²³, so the sample is 0.5 mole.
This incorrectly treats the particle count as a number of moles.

mcqs.stem: How many molecules are in 2 moles of a molecular substance?
rationales: Correct: 2 × 6.022 × 10²³ = 12.044 × 10²³ molecules.
This is the number of molecules in 1 mole, not 2 moles.
This is the number of molecules in 0.5 mole.
Two moles do not contain only two molecules.

mcqs.stem: According to the section, approximately how many amu are equal to 1.00 g?
rationales: Correct: the section states 1.00 g = 6.022 × 10²³ amu.
One amu is much smaller than one gram.
This is ten times smaller than the value given in the section.
This is not the conversion stated in the section.

mcqs.stem: In the equation 2C + O₂ → 2CO, what number of carbon atoms reacts when the equation is considered in Avogadro-sized groups as in the section?
rationales: Correct: the coefficient 2 means 2 × Nₐ carbon atoms in the stated group.
This leaves out the coefficient 2 in front of C.
This gives the oxygen molecule count multiplied by the wrong coefficient and labels it as carbon atoms.
This is the number of CO molecules formed for the stated group, not the number of carbon atoms reacting.

written.text: Why does Avogadro's number have an immense importance in chemistry?
written.finalAnswer: It connects the number of atoms or molecules, which are too small to count individually, with measurable masses in grams, allowing chemists to work out the mass ratios of reacting substances.

explain.title: Why use a very large particle count?
explain.body: Atoms and molecules are too small to count or weigh one by one. The section increases their number while keeping the reaction ratio the same, so their total masses can be expressed conveniently in grams.

explain.title: The value of Avogadro's number
explain.body: 6.022 × 10²³ is the number selected in the section. It is called Avogadro's number and is represented by Nₐ.

explain.title: A mole counts units
explain.body: Your textbook defines it this way: “Avogadro's number is the number of units in one mole of a substance.” The units may be atoms or molecules, depending on the substance.

explain.title: Using the number in calculations
explain.body: Multiply the number of moles by 6.022 × 10²³ to find units. To find moles from a number of units, divide by 6.022 × 10²³.

mistakes: Writing 6.022 × 10²³ as the number of moles instead of the number of units in one mole.
Giving a number of molecules when the question asks for atoms; remember to account for the atoms in each molecule.
Using the wrong molar mass or forgetting to convert the given mass to moles first.
Leaving out units such as mol, molecules or atoms in the final answer.
Forgetting that the coefficients in a chemical equation give the reacting particle or mole ratio.
